newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to make first official visit to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to make first official visit to Mexico.

text.p: With U.S.-Mexican tensions simmering over illegal drugs and immigration, President Bill Clinton on Monday makes his first visit to Mexico since he took office to kick off a week-long trip to Latin America.

The trip, to include Clinton's participation in a Central American summit in Costa Rica and a Caribbean summit in Barbados, is being billed by the president's aides as a celebration of a trend toward democracy in the region, with communist Cuba as the lone holdout.

"Now, we have every nation a democracy, whereas 10 years ago we were dealing in many cases with authoritarian dictatorships," said National Security Adviser Sandy Berger. "We now have governments, largely democratically elected, focusing on economic development."

In contrast to the optimism is the scourge of drug trafficking and drug-related corruption, and Clinton is expected to make the drug war a major component of his three-day visit to Mexico City and its environs.

"This drug problem is as big or bigger a problem for Mexico as it is for the United States. They will, in the end, not be able to maintain the fabric of an orderly, democratic, free society if the narco-traffickers come to dominate huge sections of their country," Clinton said on Saturday.
Clinton has worked to help Mexico by getting Congress to pass the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1994 and by arranging emergency support for its 1995 peso crisis.

This is Clinton's first trip to Mexico since he and Mrs. Clinton went to Acapulco on their honeymoon. It will be the first visit by a U.S. president to Mexico City since Jimmy Carter went there in 1979.

Clinton goes to Mexico with relations strained over U.S. criticism of corruption among high-level Mexican drug agents, and Mexican attacks on newly passed U.S. immigration laws. Mexico is traditionally sensitive to any hint that its sovereignty is being breached by its northern neighbour.
U.S. officials expected only modest agreements toward increased cooperation on the drug war to come from the visit.

One long-standing dispute that Clinton would like to resolve is whether agents from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency can carry their weapons while in Mexico. U.S. officials asked for permission after murders in the autumn of 1996 of Mexican officers who had been working with U.S. agents.

President Ernesto Zedillo appeared to rule out any agreement on the sidearm problem. The New York Times said Zedillo, in an interview with American reporters on Friday, said he wanted to cooperate in the drug war.
"But when I'm told that some people in the U.S. government would like to see their agents armed in Mexico, I say no! The answer is no! No further discussion!" he said.
The two countries have tensions over immigration as well. Mexico fears new U.S. legislation cracking down on illegal immigrants will spark mass deportations.
Clinton said some tensions are inevitable but that something must be done to control illegal immigrants.

"If we have laws and people wait in line, sometimes for years, to come to this country, it is wrong not to try to be tough to stop those who seek to evade those laws and come in ahead of their ordinary time. That's not right," Clinton said.
A number of top officials were to accompany Clinton, including Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Attorney General Janet Reno and drug czar Barry McCaffrey.
Mrs. Clinton was to depart on Sunday to tour the Yucatan Peninsula then fly to Mexico City on Monday night to meet up with her husband, who is still on crutches following knee surgery.
